articles.title: Redox-responsive peptide assemblies for precision theranostic.
articles.abstract: Redox biology represents a universal molecular language that encodes biochemical gradients, distinguishing healthy from diseased tissues with significant precision. The convergence of redox signaling and peptide self-assembly results in a versatile chemical framework for next-generation theranostics. Peptides, programmable, biocompatible, and hierarchically organized, can translate subtle oxidative cues into structural transitions, functional activation, and real-time diagnostic output. Redox-responsive molecular assemblies leveraging disulfide exchange, thiol oxidation, methionine sulfoxidation, and dithiane chemistry enable dynamic assembly, phase transition, or disintegration based on local redox potential. Redox dysregulation, encompassing reactive oxygen species and reactive nitrogen species imbalance, glutathione depletion, and iron-driven lipid peroxidation - governs diverse pathologies from cancer to neurodegeneration. In parallel, beyond traditional delivery platforms, redox-activated phase-separating peptides forming coacervate microdroplets have emerged as versatile drug vectors with high-capacity recruitment of nucleic acids, proteins, and small molecules, with cytosolic release triggered by glutathione. These condensate-like materials exhibit rapid and very high encapsulation efficiency, intracellular uptake, and redox-coded responsiveness. Additionally, imaging probes coupling redox-triggered bond cleavage with optical or magnetic signal activation allow real-time visualization of redox landscapes during therapy. From a translational perspective, progress is accelerated by advances in large-scale solid-phase peptide synthesis, redox-stable manufacturing workflows, and evolving regulatory frameworks. Future redox-responsive peptide coacervates are envisioned as programmable "chemical processors" that sense oxidative flux, interpret biochemical input, and deliver microenvironments-specific outputs. Such adaptive, information-rich architectures position peptide-based redox nanotheranostics as an emerging class of biomaterials capable of combining therapeutic action with the dynamic redox logic of diseases.

articles.title: Immunometabolism of tumor-associated macrophages in driving colorectal cancer.
articles.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality. Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) regulate CRC progression through functional polarization and metabolic reprogramming. Beyond the classical M1/M2 paradigm, single-cell and spatial studies reveal heterogeneous TAM subsets with distinct metabolic programs, spatial organization, and stage-dependent functions. This review delineates how TAM metabolic reprogramming drives CRC via metabolite-induced PD-L1 expression, oncogenic signaling, and crosstalk with chronic inflammation and gut microbiota. We emphasize spatial metabolic heterogeneity, TAM-tumor metabolic symbiosis, the stage-dependent duality of M2-like macrophages in colitis versus CRC, and pathogen-driven cross-kingdom manipulation. Clinical evidence linking TAM metabolic features to molecular subtypes, metastasis, prognosis, and treatment response is integrated, and methodological challenges in distinguishing true metabolic reprogramming from phenotypic changes are discussed. Therapeutic strategies targeting TAM metabolism, including small molecules, chemotherapeutics, TCM, nanomedicine, probiotics, and combinations, are summarized, offering precise TAM reprogramming to reverse immunosuppression and overcome CRC therapeutic bottlenecks.

articles.title: Polypharmacological targeting of atopic dermatitis by natural products: A mechanism-driven systematic review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Atopic dermatitis (AD) involves interconnected disturbances in epidermal barrier function, immune regulation, microbial homeostasis, and neuroimmune itch. Natural products influence several of these processes, but their mechanistic and clinical evidence remains fragmented. PURPOSE: To assess natural product-based interventions for AD within a polypharmacological framework and identify priorities for clinical translation. STUDY DESIGN: Mechanism-driven systematic review with qualitative narrative synthesis. METHODS: PubMed and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception to March 2026. Eligible studies evaluated isolated natural compounds, characterized extracts or formulations, natural lipids, or microbe-derived interventions in patients with AD or validated experimental models. Evidence was synthesized by chemotype, pathological axis, molecular target or pathway, study design, and translational relevance. RESULTS: A total of 156 original studies were retained. Reported effects clustered around epidermal differentiation and lipid homeostasis, inflammatory signaling, host-microbial interactions, and pruriceptive pathways. Preclinical studies provided mechanistic evidence for barrier-restorative, immunomodulatory, microbiome-related, and antipruritic effects involving multiple pathways. Clinical studies reported improvements in disease severity, barrier-related measures, pruritus, and quality of life, although findings varied across interventions and study designs. Direct target engagement, exposure-response relationships, and contributions of individual constituents in multicomponent preparations remained incompletely resolved. CONCLUSION: Natural products provide a pharmacologically diverse basis for intervention across interconnected AD pathways. Current evidence supports therapeutic potential and multitarget activity, although polypharmacological synergy, comparative efficacy, and long-term safety require further validation. Clinical translation requires reproducible product characterization, direct mechanistic validation, pharmacokinetic assessment, human-relevant models, and well-designed clinical studies.

articles.title: Ciprofol versus propofol for painless gastrointestinal endoscopy: a dose-stratified systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: We compared ciprofol with propofol for painless gastrointestinal endoscopy, focusing on dose, recovery, induction, satisfaction, and adverse events. METHODS: PubMed and Embase were searched through May 2026 for randomized controlled trials in adults undergoing painless gastrointestinal endoscopy. We pooled weighted mean differences (WMDs) for continuous outcomes and risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251088249). RESULTS: Eleven trials (2,084 participants) met the criteria. Recovery was statistically longer with ciprofol (WMD 0.83 min, 95% CI 0.16 to 1.49; P = 0.01), but the absolute difference was under 1 min; the difference was observed at 0.4 and 0.5 mg/kg. Induction time and physician and patient satisfaction did not differ significantly. Ciprofol was associated with fewer reported episodes of hypotension (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.72-0.90), injection pain (RR 0.13, 95% CI 0.08-0.22), respiratory depression (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.27-0.83), and hypoxemia (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.42-0.96). CONCLUSION: Ciprofol and propofol produced broadly comparable procedural outcomes. The apparent advantages for selected adverse events and the dose-related recovery pattern are uncertain because all trials were conducted in China, several pooled outcomes were highly heterogeneous, outcome definitions varied, and publication bias was possible. The dose-stratified findings are exploratory, and the results are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger international trials. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251088249, identifier PROSPERO CRD420251088249.

articles.title: Natural product-derived interventions for reversing multidrug resistance in resistant K562 leukemia cells: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Multidrug resistance remains a major barrier to effective chemotherapy for leukemia. Natural product-derived interventions have been widely investigated as modulators of drug resistance in adriamycin- or doxorubicin-resistant K562 cell models, but their quantitative reversal effects remain heterogeneous. METHODS: In vitro studies evaluating natural product-derived interventions in resistant K562 leukemia sublines were synthesized. The primary meta-analytic endpoint was IC50-based reversal fold (RF), analyzed as log (RF) using an inverse-variance random-effects model. Subgroup, sensitivity, leave-one-out, and small-study-effect analyses were performed. Mechanistic outcomes related to transporter modulation, drug accumulation, apoptosis, and signaling pathways were summarized descriptively. RESULTS: Twenty-eight in vitro studies were included, and 19 IC50-based study-level effects were entered into the primary meta-analysis. The pooled RF was 6.31 (95% CI: 4.77-8.36), representing an overall chemosensitization signal across the restricted quantitative dataset. Subgroup analysis showed pooled RF values of 5.71 for K562/A02, 4.90 for K562/ADM, and 8.91 for K562/ADR. Heterogeneity was high (I2 = 97.7%), indicating substantial variability across resistant-cell sublines, intervention types, substrate drugs, and experimental conditions. Sensitivity analyses confirmed that the pooled effect remained positive, although exclusion of high-effect studies reduced the pooled RF to 4.51. Trim-and-fill analysis produced an adjusted pooled RF of 5.48 (95% CI: 3.87-7.76). Across individual studies, reported mechanisms included ABC transporter modulation, increased intracellular anthracycline accumulation, reduced efflux, restoration of apoptosis, and modulation of PI3K/Akt, NF-κB, and Nrf2/ARE signaling. CONCLUSION: Across the heterogeneous studies, the common IC50-based endpoint showed an overall chemosensitization signal; however, this pooled summary does not imply a shared pharmacological action or potency across chemically distinct metabolites. Effect magnitude and mechanisms remained specific to individual metabolites, resistant-cell sublines, substrate drugs, doses, and molecular targets.

articles.title: TRPV3 drives lung injury by sensing inflammatory signals to disrupt alveolar epithelial barrier and promote inflammation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Pulmonary inflammation is a central pathological feature of many respiratory diseases. Transient receptor potential vanilloid 3 (TRPV3), a non-selective cation channel abundantly expressed in the skin, nerve and lung tissues, is involved in itch, skin inflammation and barrier regulation. However, its function in the pulmonary system remains elusive. We aimed to determine whether and how TRPV3 is involved in pulmonary inflammation. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and carvacrol were used to model acute lung injury (ALI) in C57BL/6J mice. Histology, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid analysis, qPCR, Western blotting, immunofluorescence, Ca2+ imaging, transepithelial electrical resistance and FITC-dextran permeability assays were used to assess inflammatory cell infiltration, cytokine expression, intracellular Ca2+ changes and epithelial barrier integrity. KEY RESULTS: TRPV3 expression is markedly up-regulated in lung tissues of ALI mice. Pharmacological activation of TRPV3 by carvacrol triggers features of ALI. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of TRPV3 significantly attenuated LPS- or carvacrol-induced lung injury. Activating TRPV3 in cultured alveolar epithelial cells increased intracellular Ca2+, boosted cytokine/chemokine production, disrupted tight junctions, reduced transepithelial electrical resistance and increased epithelial permeability. TNF-α augmented TRPV3 Ca2+ responses, and inhibition of TRPV3 activity or suppression of TRPV3 expression abolished TNF-α-induced production of cytokines/chemokines and tight junction disruption. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: TRPV3 senses inflammatory signals to augment inflammation and disrupt tight junctions in alveolar epithelial cells, making it a promising molecular target to develop treatments for pulmonary inflammation.

articles.title: Pharmacological features of mesoionic compounds: antitumoral effects and bioenergetic disruption of sydnones and 1,3,4-thiadiazolium derivatives.
articles.abstract: Mesoionic compounds are five-membered heterocyclic betaines that cannot be satisfactorily represented by a single covalent or polar structure. Because their positive and negative charges are delocalized over separate regions of the ring, they yield a net-neutral molecule with a high dipole moment. This unique electronic configuration confers amphiphilic character and pronounced affinity for biological membranes, including mitochondria, underlying a broad pharmacological profile that includes antitumoral, anti-inflammatory and analgesic activities. Among the several mesoionic scaffolds, sydnones (1,2,3-oxadiazolium-5-olate) and 1,3,4-thiadiazolium derivatives have been the most extensively studied, drawing particular attention to their pronounced antineoplastic activity against melanoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, breast cancer and glioblastoma models. Their anticancer effects are closely linked to mitochondrial bioenergetic disruption, including uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation, inhibition of respiratory complexes, dissipation of the mitochondrial membrane potential, and stimulation of F1Fo-ATPase activity, which together cause ATP depletion, redox imbalance, and apoptosis induction. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the structural features that govern these biological properties, the antitumor efficacy of sydnones and thiadiazolium derivatives across various cancer models, and the underlying mitochondrial mechanisms. By integrating chemical, pharmacological, and bioenergetic perspectives, this article highlights the potential of mesoionic compounds as versatile scaffolds for the anticancer drug development, emphasizing their preclinical antitumoral activities, the mechanisms related to cell bioenergetics, and the challenges to improve the bioviability through nanotechnologies.

articles.title: Tirofiban after intravenous thrombolysis in acute ischemic stroke patients: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract: Early antiplatelet therapy after intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) for acute ischemic stroke remains controversial because of concerns regarding hemorrhagic complications. Tirofiban, a reversible glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist, may reduce platelet-mediated rethrombosis and improve reperfusion after thrombolysis. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the efficacy and safety of early intravenous tirofiban following IVT. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception through May 2026. RCTs comparing early intravenous tirofiban versus standard care or placebo after IVT were included. Outcomes included functional independence (modified Rankin Scale [mRS] 0-2), excellent outcome (mRS 0-1), symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH), any intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), and 90-day mortality. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. Six randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1787 patients were included. Tirofiban significantly increased the likelihood of achieving functional independence at 90 days (RR, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.03-1.25; P = 0.019). Although tirofiban showed a trend toward improving excellent functional outcome, the difference was not statistically significant (RR, 1.21; 95% CI, 0.95-1.56; P = 0.080). No significant differences were observed in symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (RR, 1.72; 95% CI, 0.57-5.19; P = 0.265), any intracranial hemorrhage (RR, 1.17; 95% CI, 0.72-1.90; P = 0.453), or 90-day mortality (RR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.59-1.45; P = 0.668). Sensitivity analyses demonstrated robust findings across all outcomes. Early intravenous tirofiban following thrombolysis was associated with improved functional recovery without a significant increase in mortality or intracranial hemorrhage on a relative scale. Although a 1% absolute increase in symptomatic ICH was observed, the difference was not statistically significant. These findings support further investigation of tirofiban as an adjunct to thrombolysis in selected patients with acute ischemic stroke.

articles.title: Rational selection of lipid nanocarriers for topical corticosteroid delivery.
articles.abstract: Topical corticosteroids remain central to treating psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, eczema, and related inflammatory dermatoses; however, their effectiveness is often limited by poor lesion-specific delivery, short residence time, variable skin retention, and local or systemic adverse effects. The key challenge is not simply to increase corticosteroid penetration, but to deliver the drug to the appropriate skin layer and retain it there for long enough to achieve therapeutic effects. Lipid nanocarriers may help by modulating drug loading, release, retention, skin hydration, and penetration depth through materials that interact favourably with the skin barrier. This review evaluates the major lipid nanocarriers explored for topical corticosteroid delivery with respect to epidermal retention, dermal targeting, sustained release, and, where justified, deeper dermal delivery. It develops a target-matched selection framework and applies a Quality by Design approach linking disease context and target skin layer to product attributes, process variables, and scale-up requirements. No single lipid nanocarrier is universally optimal. Nanostructured lipid carriers are best supported when epidermal retention and sustained cutaneous residence are the main goals, whereas vesicular systems may be more suitable when controlled dermal access is required. Carrier choice should therefore be guided by disease context, target skin layer, and transport behaviour rather than penetration enhancement alone.

articles.title: Re-examination of Hermann J. Muller's 1927 Nobel Prize research: The ClB model validity, the Mavor precedent, and the reverse mutation mirage.
articles.abstract: Muller was awarded the 1946 Nobel Prize for his 1927 discovery of X-ray-induced gene mutations in Drosophila melanogaster. This paper re-examines the 1926-1927 experimental framework of this research, demonstrating that Muller's biological model was structurally incapable of isolating single-gene transmutations. Furthermore, we examine the Mavor precedent: between 1921 and 1924 during which James Mavor published quantitative experiments in Science and Genetics demonstrating that X-rays induced transmissible chromosomal alterations. To claim priority over Mavor and secure scientific primacy, Muller established an exacting standard-demanding proof of "gene transmutation" rather than crude chromosomal damage-a standard Muller claimed to have met, but which his ClB assay fundamentally failed to deliver. We delineate the hierarchy of criticism between dose execution and experimental design. The present findings demonstrate the more foundational critique that Muller's assay model was structurally inappropriate and incapable of detecting single-gene mutations under any dose regime. The paper also explores important confounding environmental laboratory conditions during the time of the Nobel Prize research concerning how this may have had significant effects on the quality of the experimental findings and their interpretation. Finally, we explore the epistemological paradox of how this century-long misinterpretation persisted into the molecular era, evaluating Muller's revised standing as a brilliant methodological engineer who constructed an unyielding paradigm that shaped regulatory toxicology for generations.

articles.title: Inhalation therapies in interstitial lung diseases.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Fibrosing interstitial lung diseases (ILDs), including Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis (PPF), impose substantial clinical and societal burdens due to irreversible lung function decline, limited therapeutic options, and poor survival. Current oral antifibrotics, while effective in slowing progression, are hampered by severe gastrointestinal side effects and high discontinuation rates, emphasizing the need for better-tolerated treatments. AREAS COVERED: This review summarizes the therapeutic limitations of existing antifibrotics, emphasizing the challenges posed by systemic exposure. We discuss recent and ongoing clinical trials with inhaled antifibrotics, the associated inhalable formulation challenges and characteristics required to align drug performance with the pathobiology of pulmonary fibrosis. We further outline advances in device technologies and drug delivery strategies for efficient drug deposition to the lungs, together with the emerging preclinical pipeline involving biologics and nanoparticles. EXPERT OPINION: The transition to inhaled antifibrotic therapy represents a promising evolution in ILD management. By achieving high local drug concentrations with markedly reduced systemic exposure, this approach has the potential to improve the limitations of oral antifibrotics. As phase-2 and phase-3 trial results emerge, the clinical success of these therapies will depend on optimized formulation and delivery strategies.

articles.title: Resistance mechanisms and reversal strategies of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors in melanoma.
articles.abstract: Programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)/programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) immune checkpoint inhibitors have redefined the therapeutic landscape of advanced melanoma, establishing a first-line standard of care that markedly prolongs patient survival. Nevertheless, primary and acquired resistance remain the principal barriers to durable clinical benefit: approximately 40%-55% of patients exhibit primary resistance to PD-1 monotherapy inhibitors, while 25%-30% of initial responders develop acquired resistance during treatment. Resistance arises from multidimensional, interconnected mechanisms spanning tumor-intrinsic alterations, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment remodeling, metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming, and systemic modulators including the gut microbiota. By linking antigen recognition, spatiotemporal regulation, and clinical translation, this review provides a mechanistic framework for understanding PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor resistance in melanoma. This review aimed to systematically evaluate the evidentiary basis for resistance-reversal strategies-encompassing immune combinations, targeted agents, cellular therapies, and localized interventions-and consolidate hierarchical biomarker systems with translational potential. Critical gaps in clinical applicability, including patient selection, treatment sequencing, and combination-related toxicity, are discussed. Finally, the review highlights unresolved challenges and future directions to guide precision optimization of melanoma immunotherapy.

articles.title: Natural metabolites targeting macrophage polarization for non-small cell lung cancer therapy: a review of mechanisms and applications based on chemical classification.
articles.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for roughly 85% of lung cancer cases and is a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Reprogramming tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) from a pro-tumor M2 phenotype to an anti-tumor M1 phenotype has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy. This review examines naturally occurring metabolites that modulate TAM polarization in NSCLC, organized into eight chemical classes: flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, polysaccharides, saponins, stilbenoids, lignans, and phenolic acids. A recurring finding is that these compounds converge on shared signaling pathways, particularly PI3K/Akt/mTOR, NF-κB, and STAT family members, while each class also displays distinct mechanistic tendencies. Flavonoids couple redox modulation with immune effects. Alkaloids engage multiple targets but carry dose-dependent toxicity. Terpenoids show strong tumor microenvironment penetration and synergy with immune checkpoint inhibitors. Polysaccharides act through membrane receptors such as Toll-like receptors and Dectin-1. Saponins largely center on AMPK signaling. The remaining classes, though supported by fewer studies, point to MDSC regulation and context-dependent effects. Multi-component plant extracts and traditional Chinese medicine formulas also influence TAM polarization and have reached adjuvant clinical use. Delivery platforms such as nanoparticles, hydrogels, and exosomes are being developed to address poor bioavailability. Translation remains limited by a lack of trials with TAM-specific endpoints, an oversimplified M1/M2 framework, and the need for standardized pharmacokinetic and targeting assessments. Future progress will require biopsy-based TAM phenotyping, biomarker-driven patient stratification, and delivery systems matched to metabolite properties.

articles.title: Targeting the Correa's cascade of gastric cancer: the potential role of phytochemicals and autophagy modulation.
articles.abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) development follows a sequential and complex pathophysiological process known as Correa's cascade, progressing from chronic gastritis (active or inactive) to precancerous lesions (intestinal metaplasia (IM) and dysplasia) and ultimately to adenocarcinoma. Current GC therapies have limited efficacy and high recurrence rates. Autophagy, a cellular self-degradation mechanism that removes damaged or harmful components, plays a critical role in maintaining cellular homeostasis. Phytochemicals, owing to their low toxicity and multi-target pharmacological properties, exhibit anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, antioxidant, and anticancer activities, and certain phytochemicals have shown potential in suppressing GC progression. In the inflammatory stage, metabolites such as berberine (an alkaloid) and chlorogenic acid (a phenolic acid) modulate autophagy by regulating the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT/mTOR pathway: upstream activation of PI3K leads to AKT phosphorylation, which subsequently inhibits the downstream autophagy-related genes Unc-51-like kinase (ULK1) and Beclin-1, while these phytochemicals can reverse this inhibition to reduce inflammatory cytokine secretion and promote ulcer healing. In the precancerous stage, agents such as ginsenoside Rg3 and astragaloside IV (terpenoids) regulate autophagy through the PI3K/AKT axis and by influencing p62/sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1), an autophagy adaptor that links upstream microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3)-interacting partners to downstream ubiquitinated substrates-thereby restoring autophagic flux and preventing malignant transformation. In the cancer stage, phytochemicals from various subclasses (phenolics, alkaloids, and terpenoids) target the core autophagy machinery: they suppress upstream PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling (with mTOR directly inhibiting the initiation complex formed by ULK1, ATG13, and FIP200), induce the expression of Beclin-1 and ATG family proteins, promote the conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II, and enhance autophagosome formation. Consequently, these metabolites inhibit GC cell proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis while inducing apoptosis and increasing chemosensitivity. From a clinical translation perspective, the consistent observation that pharmacological inhibition of cytoprotective autophagy enhances phytochemical-induced apoptosis suggests a rational combination strategy: pairing a phytochemical that induces cytoprotective autophagy with an approved autophagy inhibitor such as hydroxychloroquine. This approach has been tested in vitro for curcumin, quercetin, and berberine but not yet in animal models or clinical trials. Given the established safety profiles of these agents individually, such combinations could be rapidly tested in preclinical gastric cancer models and, if successful, progressed to early-phase clinical trials as adjuncts to standard chemotherapy. Moreover, ongoing clinical trials of berberine for gastrointestinal metaplasia and of resveratrol for chemotherapy toxicity reduction provide existing clinical frameworks onto which autophagy endpoint measurements could be incorporated. These findings highlight the potential of autophagy-targeting phytochemicals as promising strategies for GC prevention and treatment, offering valuable insights for clinical translation. Moreover, targeting autophagy with phytochemicals represents a promising avenue for future drug development, potentially enabling personalized combination therapies to overcome chemoresistance and improve long-term outcomes for patients with gastric cancer.

articles.title: Proanthocyanidins in immune-mediated inflammatory diseases: molecular mechanisms and therapeutic potential.
articles.abstract: Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs), a heterogeneous group of disorders, are characterized by chronic inflammation and subsequent organ damage, encompassing diverse conditions like atopic dermatitis (AD), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) - which includes Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). These chronic diseases mainly stem from inappropriate or excessive immune responses. In recent years, the incidence of IMIDs has been increasing. Considering their frequent association with various complications, such as cardiovascular diseases, cognitive impairment, metabolic disorders, and high-level disabilities, IMIDs have emerged as a major medical challenge. Proanthocyanidins (PCs), also known as condensed tannins, are among the most abundant polyphenols in the human diet. Owing to their health-protective activities, they have attracted extensive research interest. These compounds are commonly found in plants, including fruits, nuts, bark, chocolate, wine, as well as some plant seeds and flowers. A multitude of studies have demonstrated that PCs possess a wide range of pharmacological properties, such as antioxidant effects, anti-inflammatory action, immune regulation, cardiovascular benefits, and antineoplastic effects. It has been demonstrated that PCs, as natural plant compounds, are safe and rare of notable adverse effects. Their extensive range of biological activities has facilitated their applications in treating various IMIDs. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the diverse biological activities of PCs and their favorable roles in common IMIDs, while also elucidating the underlying mechanisms involved in IMIDs.

articles.title: Astragaloside IV in hepatocellular carcinoma: repolarizing macrophages to reprogram the tumor microenvironment.
articles.abstract: The establishment of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) represents a central mechanism underlying the failure of conventional therapies and resistance to immunotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), as the most abundant immune cell population within this microenvironment, play a pivotal role in establishing immunosuppression, promoting angiogenesis, and driving therapeutic resistance through their polarization toward the M2 phenotype. Astragaloside IV (AS-IV), the principal bioactive constituent of the traditional Chinese medicine Astragalus membranaceus, has recently been recognized for its remarkable immunomodulatory properties. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in understanding the multi-dimensional mechanisms through which AS-IV modulates M2 macrophage polarization. At the signaling pathway level, AS-IV undermines the molecular basis of macrophage polarization by inhibiting signal transducer and activator of transcription 3/6 (STAT3/STAT6) phosphorylation and modulating phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mammalian target of rapamycin (PI3K/Akt/mTOR) and AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling cascades. At the metabolic level, it influences the metabolic reprogramming of macrophages, thereby altering their functional phenotypes. At the epigenetic level, it may interfere with processes such as histone modifications, thereby attenuating the "memory" of M2 polarization. This multi-layered regulation promotes the reprogramming of TAMs from a pro-tumorigenic M2 phenotype toward an anti-tumor M1-like phenotype, thereby systematically remodeling the HCC immune microenvironment-restoring effector T cell function, reducing immunosuppressive cell infiltration, inhibiting angiogenesis, and ameliorating the fibrotic barrier. This review aims to provide a systematic framework for understanding the immunomodulatory mechanisms of AS-IV and offer a theoretical foundation for the development of novel natural product-based immunotherapeutic strategies for HCC.

articles.title: ALKBH5 inhibitors for cancer therapy: molecular docking, challenges and future prospects.
articles.abstract: N6-Methyladenosine (m6A), the most abundant internal modification of eukaryotic mRNA, is dynamically reversed by the FeII/α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase ALKBH5, a key m6A "eraser" that regulates target mRNA fate through demethylation. ALKBH5 is aberrantly overexpressed in acute myeloid leukemia, glioblastoma, breast cancer and other malignancies, where it sustains oncogenic programs, establishing it as a promising epitranscriptomic drug target. At present, ALKBH5 inhibitor development lags behind that of FTO, with selective agents only recently emerging through covalent inhibitors such as compound 33, 25 and 40, though no clinically available ALKBH5-targeted drug yet exists. This review summarizes the biological functions, structural features, and molecular docking between reported inhibitors and target proteins of ALKBH5. Current challenges, including selectivity over homologous dioxygenases, structural optimization and resistance mechanisms, are critically discussed, alongside future perspectives on structure-guided design, combination regimens and clinical translation. This review provides a medicinal chemistry framework to accelerate the discovery of potent and selective ALKBH5 inhibitors for precision cancer therapy.

articles.title: Beyond angiogenesis: the paradoxical emerging pro-tumorigenic role of Thrombospondin-2.
articles.abstract: The tumor microenvironment is a complex ecosystem where the extracellular matrix serves as a dynamic signaling hub and regulates tumorigenesis. Thrombospondin-2 (THBS2), a matricellular extracellular matrix protein, has traditionally been regarded as an inhibitor of angiogenesis. However, emerging evidence reveals a pleiotropic and paradoxical pro-tumorigenic role of THBS2 in several malignancies. THBS2 has been identified as a multifaceted regulator of critical mechanisms driving cancer progression including angiogenesis induction, vasculogenic mimicry, sustained proliferation, invasion, metastasis, phenotypic plasticity, and immune suppression in aggressive cancers. By modulating diverse signaling pathways, especially the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis, remodeling the collagenous architecture of the extracellular matrix, and formation of non-endothelial vascular channels, THBS2 supports tumor progression and metastasis. This minireview encompasses current research regarding the emerging molecular mechanisms by which THBS2 regulates pro-tumorigenic functions and discusses its role in resistance to therapy. The diagnostic and prognostic value of THBS2, particularly in aggressive cancers, underscores the need for the development of novel therapeutics specifically targeting this deregulated protein.

articles.title: Innate immunity and hypertension: unveiling inflammatory pathways for novel therapies.
articles.abstract: Hypertension is a leading cause of global cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, yet its primary etiology remains poorly defined. Accumulating evidence increasingly positions inflammation as a key determinant of disease progression, with both innate and adaptive immune mechanisms playing central roles. Under physiological conditions, the immune system safeguards vascular homeostasis through the coordinated activity of immune cells and soluble mediators. Cells of the innate immune system, such as natural killer cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, and neutrophils, detect pathogen- and damage-associated molecular patterns via pattern recognition receptors, while complement proteins and antimicrobial peptides serve as additional effectors of host defense. Perturbations in these pathways, however, precipitate chronic inflammation that contributes to hypertensive pathology. Engagement of toll-like and nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like receptors initiates pro-inflammatory cascades that intensify oxidative stress, impair vasodilation, and compromise endothelial function. These alterations are further propagated by activated immune cells and by complement-mediated recruitment of leukocytes, which sustain a deleterious inflammatory milieu. Collectively, these mechanisms contribute to vascular injury and perpetuate elevated blood pressure. Emerging therapies designed to target these immune-inflammatory pathways offer promising opportunities to alleviate vascular dysfunction and ultimately transform the management of hypertension by addressing its immunological underpinnings.

articles.title: Targeting lysosomal ion channels to overcome cancer treatment resistance: emerging mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
articles.abstract: Lysosomes are critical cellular organelles that not only regulate metabolic regulation but also play pivotal roles in cell death, signal transduction, and tumorigenesis. The various ion channels expressed on the lysosomal membrane are central to these physiological functions; they intricately maintain lysosomal pH homeostasis, calcium ion homeostasis, and membrane potential. Consequently, the dysregulation of these channels has emerged as a potential target of tumor cells, driving tumor cell proliferation, metastasis, apoptosis, and drug resistance. This review summarizes the structure and function of major lysosomal ion channels, emphasizing their central roles in regulating the tumor microenvironment, cell survival, and treatment resistance. Specifically, we highlight their involvement in mediating resistance to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy, elucidating the associated molecular mechanisms. Furthermore, we explore the prospects and challenges of developing targeted therapeutic strategies towards these ion channels to overcome tumor drug resistance.

articles.title: Cannabinoids in hematologic malignancies: mechanisms and therapeutic potential for overcoming drug resistance.
articles.abstract: Hematologic malignancies are highly heterogeneous diseases in which the emergence of therapy resistance remains a major obstacle to durable clinical benefit. Cannabinoids, acting through the endocannabinoid system, have drawn increasing interest because of their potential to modulate multiple resistance-associated pathways, yet the available evidence remains fragmented across disease entities, experimental models, and mechanistic frameworks. In this narrative review, we examine the molecular mechanisms by which cannabinoids may counteract drug resistance in leukemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma. We discuss their effects on ABC transporter-mediated drug efflux, mitochondrial apoptosis, redox homeostasis, endoplasmic reticulum stress and autophagy, pro-survival signaling, and tumor microenvironment-mediated protection. We also evaluate preclinical evidence for cannabinoid-based combinations with conventional chemotherapy, targeted therapies, immunotherapies, and radiotherapy. Although in vitro and animal studies indicate that cannabinoids may reverse resistant phenotypes and enhance the activity of existing treatments, the translational relevance of these findings is limited by the predominance of cell-line and xenograft models, the paucity of clinical evidence for antitumor efficacy, pharmacokinetic constraints, potential drug-drug interactions, and context-dependent effects that may be neutral or adverse in certain immunological settings. Thus, while the endocannabinoid system represents a potential therapeutic target for sensitizing resistant hematologic malignancies, clinical translation will require validation at pharmacologically achievable exposures, the use of immunocompetent and clinically relevant models, identification of predictive biomarkers, and rigorous evaluation in prospective clinical studies.

articles.title: Microbiome-aware oral drug delivery: excipient-microbiome interactions and nanocarrier design rules for predictable formulation performance.
articles.abstract: Oral drug delivery remains the predominant administration route, but formulation strategies rarely account systematically for the gut microbiome. The microbiome can alter drug metabolism, excipient behavior, nanocarrier interactions, and interpatient variability. This review integrates evidence on microbial drug metabolism, excipient-microbiome interactions, nanocarrier engineering, microbiota-responsive delivery, and experimental models. Clinically relevant examples include digoxin inactivation by Eggerthella lenta, bacterial levodopa metabolism, and microbial beta-glucuronidase-mediated irinotecan toxicity. Microbiota-degradable polysaccharides may serve as colon-targeted release triggers, whereas some surfactants and polymers may create context-dependent microbiome or barrier risks. Nanocarrier size, charge, coating, mucoadhesion, mucus penetration, biodegradability, enzyme responsiveness, and surfactant burden are treated as microbiome-interface variables. We propose an authors' evidence-informed framework comprising an excipient classification, nanocarrier design rules, microbiota-responsive decision logic, and a tiered testing roadmap. These proposals are not established regulatory classifications; they are intended to support more predictable and patient-relevant oral formulation development.

articles.title: Deciphering the mechanisms of resveratrol in knee osteoarthritis treatment: insights from bioinformatics and experimental validation.
articles.abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is the most prevalent chronic joint disorder in orthopedics, with its underlying pathogenic genes and effective treatment methods remaining unclear. Resveratrol (RES), a potent bioactive natural polyphenol, has been shown to effectively alleviate KOA; however, its complex regulatory mechanisms require further investigation. This research seeks to clarify the molecular mechanisms by which RES contributes to the treatment of KOA, utilizing a blend of bioinformatics approaches and experimental validation. First, gene expression profiles related to KOA were obtained from the GEO database. Subsequently, differential gene analysis was conducted on the samples, and modular genes linked to KOA were extracted through the application of a weighted gene co-expression network. The LASSO algorithm was utilized to identify crucial pathogenic genes in KOA, which were later confirmed using clinical samples. Targets for RES were sourced from traditional Chinese medicine databases, and the therapeutic targets for KOA treatment were determined by finding the intersection of these sources. An enrichment analysis was carried out based on the therapeutic targets identified. Molecular docking studies were conducted to further assess the binding affinity of key therapeutic genes with RES. Lastly, animal experiments were implemented to substantiate the molecular mechanisms by which RES acts in the treatment of KOA. We identified 460 module genes and 10 key predictive genes through LASSO analysis. The findings from the enrichment analysis concerning potential therapeutic targets for RES in the treatment of KOA reveal that the significant genes implicated include VEGFA, IL6, MAPK3, IL1B, CASP3, and AKT1. Subsequent validation with clinical samples revealed that IL6, MAPK3, IL1B, CASP3, and AKT1 were significantly elevated during the progression of KOA, while VEGFA was markedly reduced in the context of KOA. The outcomes of the GO and KEGG analyses suggest that the primary biological processes implicated encompass apoptosis, the FoxO signaling pathway, the IL-17 signaling pathway, cellular senescence, and the NF-κB signaling pathway. The findings from the immune infiltration analysis indicate that resting CD4 memory T cells, memory B cells, resting mast cells, eosinophils, and activated mast cells may have important functions in the immune mechanisms related to KOA. The results of animal experiments demonstrate that RES effectively inhibits the expression of inflammatory factors such as IL-6, MAPK3, IL-1β, CASP3, and AKT1 during the progression of KOA, promotes the expression of VEGFA, and concurrently suppresses the FoxO signaling pathway and the IL-17 signaling pathway, thereby reducing cartilage damage induced by MIA and delaying the progression of KOA. In summary, RES can regulate the expression of genes including VEGFA, IL-6, MAPK3, IL-1β, CASP3, and AKT1, inhibit the FoxO signaling pathway and the IL-17 signaling pathway, alleviate cartilage damage induced by MIA, and delay the progression of KOA.

articles.title: Phytochemical Profiling and Multi-Target Wound-Healing Potential of Millettia extensa (Benth.) Baker Stem Bark Extracts: Integrated Computational and Experimental Validation.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Millettia species (Fabaceae) are traditionally used across parts of Asia and Africa for managing wounds, skin infections, and inflammatory disorders. Millettia extensa (Benth.) Baker is traditionally associated with the management of wounds and inflammatory conditions. However, its stem bark has not been systematically evaluated for wound-healing activity. AIM OF THE STUDY: To investigate the wound-healing potential of methanol (MEM) and aqueous (MEA) extracts of M. extensa stem bark using integrated in-silico, in-vitro and in-vivo experimental approaches. MATERIALS AND METHODS: MEM and MEA were subjected to preliminary phytochemical screening, estimation of total phenolic and flavonoid contents, and UHPLC-ESI-QTOF-MS/MS profiling. The shortlisted phytoconstituents were subsequently analyzed using network pharmacology and molecular docking against AKT1, IL-1β, STAT3 and TNF-α, while isoliquiritigenin was further evaluated by 200-ns molecular dynamics simulation. The extracts were further evaluated for antioxidant activity using the DPPH assay, antimicrobial activity using agar well diffusion and broth microdilution assays, acute toxicity and wound-healing activity using the HaCaT scratch-wound assay, carrageenan-induced paw edema model, and excision and incision wound models. Extract-based ointments were evaluated in the topical wound-healing models. RESULTS: MEM contained higher phenolic (108.59 mg GAE/g) and flavonoid (71.84 mg QE/g) contents than MEA (49.28 mg GAE/g and 40.59 mg QE/g, respectively), with 28 and 63 tentatively annotated compounds, respectively. Network pharmacology identified 86 shared wound-healing targets, among which AKT1, TNF, STAT3, and IL-1β emerged as key hub targets. Isoliquiritigenin exhibited consistent multi-target docking affinities (-9.1 to -6.8 kcal/mol) and the isoliquiritigenin-AKT1 complex showed relatively stable conformational behaviour during the 200-ns molecular dynamics simulation. MEM showed stronger DPPH radical-scavenging activity (IC50 = 64.01 μg/mL) and greater antimicrobial activity, with a MIC of 1.56 mg/mL against P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, and S. epidermidis, compared with MEA. Both extracts showed no observable signs of acute toxicity under the tested conditions. Notably, the 10 % MEM ointment produced 99.2 ± 1.1% excision wound closure, 42.40 ± 1.83 μg/mg hydroxyproline content, and tensile strength comparable to the standard treatment. CONCLUSION: Collectively, the present findings indicate that Millettia extensa stem bark, particularly the methanol extract, has promising wound-healing potential, with the observed activity accompanied by antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and wound-repair effects. The integrated experimental and computational findings provide a basis for further mechanistic studies and validation of its potential application in topical wound management.

articles.title: Yujin Powder alleviates colonic oxidative injury in mice with dampness-heat diarrhea through the Keap1/Nrf2/GSH pathway: baicalein as a candidate key constituent.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Yujin Powder (YJP), a classic traditional Chinese medicinal formula for dampness-heat diarrhea (DHD), is widely used to treat damp-heat diarrhea in animals such as cattle and horses. However, the precise mechanisms by which YJP exerts its antioxidant effects in the treatment of DHD via the Keap1/Nrf2/GSH signaling pathway have not been fully elucidated. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to investigate the mechanisms by which YJP ameliorates oxidative injury in the colonic epithelium of DHD mice and to identify candidate active constituents potentially involved in this process. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A DHD mouse model was established and treated with YJP. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed based on hematological parameters, serum biochemical indices, blood viscosity, colonic inflammatory responses, and histopathological changes. Transcriptomic analysis was performed to characterize gene expression alterations in the colon. Mechanistic validation was conducted using qRT-PCR, Western blotting, and multiplex immunofluorescence. Furthermore, an in vitro oxidative stress model using LPS-stimulated NCM-460 cells was established to verify the antioxidant activity of baicalein, a candidate key constituent of YJP identified through virtual screening and molecular dynamics simulations. RESULTS: YJP significantly alleviated diarrhea symptoms in DHD mice, improved body weight loss, corrected metabolic disorders, reduced systemic and colonic inflammatory responses, and restored colonic epithelial integrity. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that YJP enhanced antioxidant defense by regulating the Keap1/Nrf2/GSH pathway, thereby reducing oxidative stress and epithelial injury. Through virtual screening and molecular dynamics simulations, baicalein was identified as a candidate key constituent of YJP and showed the potential to form stable interactions with both Keap1 and Nrf2. In vitro experiments further confirmed that baicalein markedly attenuated LPS-induced oxidative stress in NCM-460 cells, supporting its role as an important contributor to the antioxidant effects of YJP. CONCLUSION: YJP alleviates colonic oxidative injury in DHD mice by regulating the Keap1/Nrf2/GSH pathway, while baicalein may represent a candidate key constituent contributing to this antioxidant effect.

articles.title: Ampelopsis grossedentata alleviates vascular cognitive impairment in BCAS mice by regulating VEGFA/KDR/FGFR1-mediated angiogenesis and GSK3β/Bcl-2/Bax-mediated mitochondrial apoptosis.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Ampelopsis grossedentata (Hand.-Mazz.) W.T. Wang (vine tea) is a time-honored ethnomedicine used by the Tujia and Miao minorities in Southern China. It has traditionally been used for "clearing heat and detoxifying", "activating blood and unblocking collaterals", and "subduing liver-yang to resolve phlegm and eliminate turbidity". Its aqueous infusion is consumed as a folk remedy to alleviate vertigo, dizziness, and hypertension-related cardio-cerebrovascular symptoms. These traditional applications suggest its potential therapeutic relevance to chronic cerebral hypoperfusion-induced vascular cognitive impairment. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to investigate the protective effects and underlying mechanisms of vine tea aqueous extract against chronic cerebral hypoperfusion-induced vascular cognitive impairment, focusing on its regulation of angiogenic signaling and mitochondrial apoptosis-related pathways. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The chemical profile of vine tea aqueous extract was characterized by UPLC-Q-TOF-MS, and selected constituents were quantified. Network pharmacology and bioinformatics analysis using the GSE122063 dataset were performed to identify active constituents and candidate therapeutic targets. Molecular docking and 200-ns molecular dynamics simulations evaluated their binding stability. Male C57BL/6 mice were randomly divided into five groups (n = 20/group): Sham, Model, positive control (nimodipine, 11.7 mg/kg), VTL (100 mg/kg), and VTH (200 mg/kg). Vascular cognitive impairment was induced by microcoil-induced bilateral common carotid artery stenosis (BCAS). After a 1-week recovery period, mice received daily oral gavage for 30 days. Behavioral performance was assessed using the open field test, novel object recognition test, and Morris water maze. Cerebral perfusion, CD31-positive microvascular density, myelin integrity, neuronal morphology, neuronal apoptosis, and mitochondrial ultrastructure were assessed. Biochemical assays determined oxidative stress, ATP and lactic acid levels, while related genes and proteins were examined by RT-PCR and Western blotting. RESULTS: UPLC-Q-TOF-MS identified 31 compounds, among which dihydromyricetin, quercetin, taxifolin, aromadendrin, catechin, epigallocatechin and naringenin (predicted OB ≥ 20%, DL ≥ 0.18) were quantitatively determined. Network analysis identified seven hub targets, including a pro-angiogenic module (VEGFA, KDR, FGFR1) and an apoptosis-related module (GSK3β, RAF1, BCL2, BAX). Molecular docking and dynamics simulations supported stable interactions between the major constituents and hub targets. In BCAS mice, vine tea significantly improved cognitive behavior, restored regional cerebral blood flow (P < 0.01) and increased CD31-positive microvascular density (P < 0.05), while preserving myelin integrity (P < 0.01) and hippocampal neuron survival (P < 0.05). These benefits were accompanied by attenuated mitochondrial ultrastructural damage, increased ATP, SOD, and GSH levels, and reduced lactate and MDA content (P < 0.05), as well as decreased cleaved caspase-3/NeuN double-positive apoptotic neurons (P < 0.05). Mechanistically, VT restored VEGFA/KDR/FGFR1 expression, increased Bcl-2/Bax ratio and GSK3β phosphorylation, and normalized RAF1 hyperphosphorylation, suggesting coordinated regulation of angiogenic signaling and mitochondrial apoptosis-related pathways. CONCLUSIONS: Vine tea ameliorated cognitive deficits and hippocampal neuronal injury in BCAS mice by restoring VEGFA/KDR/FGFR1-mediated angiogenic signaling and rebalancing GSK3β/RAF1 and Bcl-2/Bax-related mitochondrial apoptotic pathways. These findings suggest vine tea as a promising multi-target ethnomedicinal candidate for vascular cognitive impairment, although the causal link between these two processes warrants further mechanistic validation.

articles.title: Sequential Stage-Specific Administration of Bushen-Tiaojing Decoctions II and III Ameliorates Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Ovarian Granulosa Cells of COH Mice by Regulating GRP75-Mediated MAM Homeostasis.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) offers a distinct therapeutic approach to infertility. Bushen-Tiaojing Decoctions II (BSTJ-II-D) and III (BSTJ-III-D; collectively, BSTJD) are clinical formulas developed by Professor Huilan Du according to the TCM theory of stage-specific treatment and are widely used in the clinical management of infertility. Previous studies have shown that sequential, stage-specific administration of these formulas can improve mitochondrial energy metabolism and increase pregnancy rates among infertile women undergoing in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer (IVF-ET). However, whether this sequential treatment improves mitochondrial function in ovarian granulosa cells (GCs) by preserving mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum membrane (MAM) homeostasis remains unclear. AIM OF THE STUDY: Glucose-regulated protein 75 (GRP75) is a key tethering protein that maintains MAM homeostasis. This study aimed to determine whether sequential, stage-specific administration of BSTJ-II-D and BSTJ-III-D ameliorates mitochondrial dysfunction in ovarian GCs by regulating GRP75-mediated MAM homeostasis. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) mouse model was established, after which animals received BSTJ-II-D and BSTJ-III-D sequentially via oral gavage. A group treated with GRP75-IN-1, a novel small-molecule compound that targets and binds GRP75, was included as a control. MAM morphology, mitochondrial bioenergetic activity, and mitochondrial biogenesis were systematically evaluated. For the in vitro experiments, human KGN ovarian granulosa-like tumor cells were transduced with a GRP75-overexpressing lentiviral construct to clarify how elevated GRP75 expression affects MAM architecture and function and subsequently influences mitochondrial homeostasis. Protein levels of GRP75, voltage-dependent anion channel 1 (VDAC1), mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU), sirtuin 1 (SIRT1), peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1α (PGC-1α), and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) were assessed in GCs. Cellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, mitochondrial Ca2+ loading, and mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) were determined using fluorescence-based assays. In addition, mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening was evaluated quantitatively by flow cytometric analysis. RESULTS: Sequential BSTJD treatment attenuated COH-induced aberrant GRP75 overexpression, restored MAM ultrastructural integrity, reduced mitochondrial oxidative stress (OS) and Ca2+ overload, and enhanced mitochondrial energy metabolism and biogenesis. Mechanistically, BSTJD increased the expression of SIRT1, PGC-1α, and Nrf2 while inhibiting activation of the PERK/ATF4 pathway, thereby alleviating endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and enhancing mitochondrial energy metabolism and biogenesis. GRP75-IN-1 reproduced the protective effects of BSTJD. Conversely, GRP75 overexpression in KGN cells disrupted MAMs and impaired mitochondrial function, further supporting GRP75 as a key mediator of the protective effects of BSTJD. CONCLUSION: Sequential BSTJD treatment preserves MAM homeostasis by suppressing aberrant GRP75 overexpression, thereby mitigating OS and mitochondrial Ca2+ overload. It also activates the SIRT1-PGC-1α-Nrf2 pathway to restore mitochondrial energy metabolism and biogenesis, ultimately ameliorating mitochondrial dysfunction in GCs. These findings provide new molecular evidence supporting the Bushen Tiaojing therapeutic approach for infertility.

articles.title: Poly(hexamethylenebiguanide) hydrochloride induces craniofacial cartilage defects and alters Wnt signaling related gene expression in zebrafish larvae.
articles.abstract: Poly(hexamethylenebiguanide) hydrochloride (PHMB) is widely used as a broad spectrum antimicrobial preservative, but its effects on craniofacial cartilage development require further characterization. Here, zebrafish were used to evaluate the developmental effects of PHMB following embryonic exposure to 0.15, 0.35, or 0.55 mg/L from 6 to 72 hours post fertilization (hpf). PHMB exposed larvae exhibited craniofacial cartilage malformations alongside general developmental abnormalities and altered locomotor behavior. These phenotypic changes were accompanied by increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) associated fluorescence, reduced proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) fluorescence intensity, and increased TUNEL positivity in the craniofacial region. qRT-PCR analysis of pooled larval heads revealed downregulation of cartilage development related genes and altered expression of inflammation related genes. Changes were also observed in the expression of Wnt signaling related genes, including β-catenin, lef1, and axin2. Furthermore, in separate rescue experiments, astaxanthin (AST) and the Wnt signaling agonist BML-284 each partially alleviated the craniofacial abnormalities. Taken together, these findings provide experimental evidence of PHMB associated craniofacial developmental toxicity under laboratory conditions, accompanied by oxidative stress related changes and altered Wnt related gene expression. General developmental toxicity may contribute to the craniofacial phenotype, and the partial pharmacological rescue does not establish pathway specific causality.

articles.title: 161Tb Radiopharmaceutical Therapy as a Treatment for RANKL-Positive Multiple Myeloma.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Denosumab, an anti-RANKL monoclonal antibody, is clinically approved for bone protection in multiple myeloma (MM) but lacks direct cytotoxic effects on tumor cells. Herein, we repurpose this well-tolerated antibody as a targeted delivery vehicle by conjugating it with the emerging radionuclide 161Tb, which emits low-energy conversion and Auger electrons with ultra-short tissue range, offering high relative biological effectiveness against single tumor cells and micrometastases. However, 161Tb-based radiopharmaceutical therapy has not been explored in MM. Our purpose is to evaluate the therapeutic potential of [161Tb]Tb-DOTA-Denosumab compared to [177Lu]Lu-DOTA-Denosumab for RANKL-positive MM. METHODS: DOTA-conjugated Denosumab was labeled with 161Tb and 177Lu. Radiochemical purity, in vitro stability and biodistribution were assessed. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in U266 and H929 subcutaneous xenograft models. Tumor volume, survival, body weight, hematologic, and biochemical parameters were monitored. Administered-activity-escalation toxicity studies were performed in tumor-free mice. RESULTS: Both radiolabeled conjugates showed high radiochemical purity (>95%), excellent in vitro stability and comparable tumor uptake. [161Tb]Tb-DOTA-Denosumab demonstrated significantly enhanced antitumor efficacy compared to [177Lu]Lu-DOTA-Denosumab at equivalent (1.85 MBq) or lower activities. In the U266 model, median survival was prolonged from 33 days (saline) to 45 days with 161Tb (1.85 MBq) versus 39 days with 177Lu (1.85 MBq). In the H929 model, median survival extended to 47 days with 161Tb (1.85 MBq) versus 31 days (saline) and 41 days with 177Lu (1.85 MBq). Toxicity studies confirmed reversible hematologic changes only at administered activities ≥3.70 MBq, with no severe organ damage. CONCLUSIONS: This is the first demonstration of 161Tb-based radiopharmaceutical therapy targeting RANKL in MM. [161Tb]Tb-DOTA-Denosumab exhibits superior antitumor efficacy and prolonged survival compared to its 177Lu-labeled counterpart. The unique Auger/conversion electron emission of 161Tb enables potent cytotoxicity against MM cells with favorable organ tolerability. These findings support 161Tb as a next-generation theranostic radionuclide for RANKL-positive malignancies and provide a strong rationale for clinical translation, highlighting the value of repurposing a clinically established antibody for radiopharmaceutical therapy.

articles.title: Development of sericin-elastin nanoblends containing resveratrol for cosmeceutical applications.
articles.abstract: Resveratrol (RSV), a high-value phytocompound upcycled from winemaking byproducts, is highly promising for cosmeceutical applications against oxidative stress due to its extraordinary antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective properties. However, its topical application is severely limited by chemical instability, poor aqueous solubility, and rapid degradation by light and oxygen. To overcome these limitations and maximize epidermal efficacy, a biocompatible nanoblend composed of sericin and elastin was developed. The sericin (4 mg/mL)/elastin (2 mg/mL) nanoblends showed an average diameter of 140 nm, a narrow size distribution, a Zeta potential of -35 mV and high stability at pH 7 and 10, as well as at temperatures between 32 °C and 37 °C. The encapsulation of RSV (0.4 mg/mL) did not affect the mean diameter and polydispersity index of the systems, allowing an entrapment efficiency of ∼30% (drug content of 0.12 mg/mL). The release profile showed a biphasic kinetic trend over time. When tested on HaCaT human keratinocytes, both single polymers and blend nanosystems demonstrated excellent tolerability, confirming the high biocompatibility of the formulation. Furthermore, RSV-loaded blend nanoparticles showed a superior cytoprotective effect compared to the free drug, a trend confirmed by DPPH, CellROX and MitoSOX assays. Finally, CompuSyn analysis validated a strong synergy between the carrier and RSV (CI < 1) with a synergistic effect at 10 µg/mL with a Dose Reduction Index (DRI) of 3.00. In conclusion, the developed sericin-elastin nanoblends containing RSV represent innovative cosmeceuticals characterized by strong antioxidant activity able to be employed for the topical treatment of skin disorders.

articles.title: CD44-targeted hyaluronic acid nanohydrogels enhance macrophage uptake and preserve the anti-inflammatory efficacy of dexamethasone.
articles.abstract: The inflammatory response is among the most critical drivers of tissue damage and systemic dysfunction. Although corticosteroids (CS) can achieve symptom remission and prevent tissue damage, systemic side effects are an issue due to the lack of targeted drug delivery. To this end, we propose a new approach to delivering CS via a hyaluronic acid (HA)-cholesterol nanohydrogel (NHs). Cholesterol, responsible for the formation of NHs, facilitates interactions with CS, while HA interacts with CD44, which is overexpressed on inflammatory cells. The aforementioned NHs were shown to efficiently load dexamethasone (DEX), with 75% drug entrapment efficiency without inducing cytotoxicity in the murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cell line. The ability of DEX to reduce inflammatory cytokine levels in lipopolysaccharide-activated RAW 264.7 cells remained intact when it was loaded into NHs. The empty NHs themselves exhibited anti-inflammatory activity, likely due to the high molecular weight of the HA used in the formulation. Finally, further investigation into the role of HA in immune cell uptake revealed significantly higher internalization by activated macrophages, driven by HA-CD44 interactions, which could enable improved cellular targeting. This nanohydrogel system offers a promising, easily manufactured, and highly biocompatible solution for anti-inflammatory drug delivery.

articles.title: Transfer learning-based multimodal prediction for efficient screening of afatinib co-amorphous systems.
articles.abstract: Most active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) are poorly water-soluble, limiting their pharmaceutical performance. Co-amorphous (CA) systems offer a promising formulation strategy, yet CA prediction remains constrained by limited labeled data and insufficient molecular representation. Here, a multimodal transfer-learning framework was developed by transferring molecular graph representations from a larger co-crystal dataset and integrating graph, DFT and SMILES information for small-sample CA prediction. The model achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.924 and an MCC of 0.771. Compared with existing AI-assisted CA prediction approaches, this framework combines cross-domain knowledge transfer with complementary molecular representations to address the limited-data challenge. Using afatinib (AF) as a model API, four AF-based CA systems were prepared by ball milling. Solid-state characterization supported amorphous CA formation, and dimer-level quantum-chemical calculations supported the plausibility of favorable local AF-co-former interaction motifs. The CA systems showed pH-dependent apparent solubility advantages and greater dissolution extents than Crystal AF. Under dry storage conditions, the CA systems maintained their amorphous state and morphology. CCK-8 assays revealed differences in HCC827 cell viability inhibition among the tested samples. Overall, this study establishes an AI-assisted approach for CA co-former screening and experimental prioritization, providing a practical strategy for formulation development of poorly soluble drugs.

articles.title: Glycocalyx-binding and cell-penetrating peptide-modified nanomicelles for enhanced ocular delivery of quercetin and retinal protection in a dAMD model.
articles.abstract: Dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD) is a highly prevalent degenerative retinal disease. Quercetin, a bioactive ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine, can mitigate the oxidative stress that helps drive dAMD; however, its low water solubility and poor corneal permeability limit its efficacy. We developed dual-functional polymeric micelles (PMs) co-conjugated with a glycocalyx-binding peptide (GBP) and a cell-penetrating peptide (TAT) for the enhanced topical ocular delivery of quercetin (QUE), named GT-PMs/QUE. The GT-PMs/QUE exhibited a particle size of 46.25 ± 3.05 nm and a zeta potential of -5.64 ± 0.92 mV. GT-PMs exhibited significantly higher cellular uptake efficiency than the unmodified group (PMs) and single-peptide modified groups (GBP-PMs and TAT-PMs). In the sodium iodate-induced oxidative damage model of adult retinal pigment epithelial cell line-19 (ARPE-19) cells, the GT-PMs/QUE treatment group showed significantly reduced ROS and MDA levels along with markedly increased SOD, CAT, and GSH activities that approached normal control levels compared to the model group. In a mouse model of dAMD, GT-PMs/QUE greatly improved the bioavailability of quercetin delivered via eye drop administration and attenuated sodium iodate-induced retinal damage. This study provides a theoretical and experimental basis for enhanced ocular delivery of quercetin and protection against dAMD-related retinal damage.

articles.title: Are we selecting the right model compounds for advanced formulation research?
articles.abstract: Numerous advanced-formulation papers begin with the same problem statement: "30-40% of marketed drugs, 70-75% of clinical candidates and 90% of new chemical entities are poorly soluble in water". However, these figures are not fully supported by data and citations. We traced these numbers back to their original sources and reassessed them against the current API landscape. The 30-40% value was derived from a 2006 analysis of top selling drugs. Reassessing the top selling drugs in 2025 reveals a marked increase: about 55% of the orally administered small molecules now fall into the practically insoluble category. The 70-75% and 90% claims could only be traced to conference presentations and a review abstract with no underlying data. We further argue that the Biopharmaceutics Classification System categorization is not an intrinsic property of an API since it shifts depending on dose, particle size and formulation, i.e., no compound can be classified without considering the formulation and dose. A Scopus analysis showed that the APIs most frequently used as poorly soluble model compounds are the NSAIDs, antifungals and compounds, such as carbamazepine, carvedilol and simvastatin. The majority of these "poorly solubles" are in fact completely absorbed in vivo with no solubility issues at all. As more relevant alternatives to the above-mentioned compounds, we propose and briefly review ten marketed non-oncology APIs with unresolved dissolution and solubility limitations that would make better model compounds for advanced formulation research.

articles.title: A GLP-1/apelin dual receptor agonist shows neuroprotective effects in the MPTP mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
articles.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a chronic disorder with no disease-modifying treatment available. The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) class of drugs is on the market to treat diabetes and obesity. GLP-1 drugs have also shown neuroprotective effects in animal models and clinical trials in PD patients. Apelin (APJ) is an adipokine peptide hormone with neuroprotective actions in preclinical studies. Here, we test the effects of a rationally designed bifunctional peptide, namely ELA (exendin-4-linker-apelin), in the MPTP mouse model of PD. The single GLP-1 receptor agonist liraglutide was used as a comparator. Motor activity was improved by both drugs (open field, pole test, Rotarod), and the inflammation response was reduced (activation of microglia and astrocytes, pro-inflammatory cytokine levels). In addition, synapse numbers were improved in the striatum (Golgi strain, TEM), expression of synapse-associated proteins was enhanced, alongside reduced expression of genes that increase mitochondrial fission. Mitochondrial fusion gene expressions (Opa1, Mfn2, Drp1) and mitochondrial morphology were also normalized (TEM). ELA was superior to liraglutide in some, but not all, parameters measured. The results suggest that the rational design of bifunctional peptides targeting both GLP-1 and APJ pathways-with optimized pharmacokinetics and enhanced blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability-merits further investigation as a strategy for developing more effective treatments for PD.

articles.title: NuPath, a higher-sensitivity TRUPATH-derived biosensor, expands detection of basal and agonist-induced GPCR activation.
articles.abstract: Bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) biosensors allow direct quantification of heterotrimeric G protein activation downstream of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), although restricted dynamic range can limit the detection of subtle, subunit-specific, or constitutively active signalling. We engineered NuPath, a TRUPATH-based biosensor in which Renilla luciferase 8 (RLuc8) within Gα was substituted with NanoLuc luciferase (nLuc) and enhanced yellow fluorescent protein (eYFP) replaced green fluorescent protein 2 (GFP2) fused to Gγ, while preserving the original sensor insertion architecture. NuPath is adapted for use in conventional 96-well plate format and supports direct, no-transfer readouts after receptor expression, whether receptors are introduced transiently or via stable cell lines, thereby simplifying experimental procedures. Side-by-side comparisons of matched NuPath and TRUPATH systems were performed across six GPCRs, Gαi2, GαOA, GαsL, and Gα11, and a range of Gβγ dimers. NuPath produced approximately 3- to 14-fold greater maximal agonist responses with Gαi2, GαsL, and Gα11, whereas GαOA sensors produced responses of broadly comparable magnitude with lower variability. The broadened dynamic range uncovered receptor-dependent variations in Gβγ pairing that were largely undetectable in TRUPATH measurements. NuPath further enabled detection of inverse agonist-mediated suppression of constitutive signalling at the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHSR) by liver-expressed antimicrobial peptide 2 (LEAP2), an effect not discernible using TRUPATH. AlphaFold 3 structural models suggested reduced donor-acceptor separation and diminished displacement of the Gα α-helical domain in NuPath compared with equivalent TRUPATH complexes. Collectively, these results position NuPath as a robust, modular enhancement of TRUPATH for resolving agonist-driven, Gβγ-specific, and constitutive GPCR signalling.

articles.title: Alnustone ameliorates atopic dermatitis by rebalancing TAp63/ΔNp63 to upregulate filaggrin and restore skin barrier function.
articles.abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic, pruritic, erythematous skin condition with skin barrier dysfunction, driven largely by filaggrin (FLG) deficiency; however, direct FLG-targeting therapeutics remains lacking. To identify novel natural products capable of enhancing FLG expression, we screened an in-house natural product library using a dual-luciferase reporter assay in HaCaT keratinocytes, which revealed that alnustone dose-dependently activated the human FLG promoter. RT-qPCR and Western blot analysis confirmed that alnustone upregulated FLG mRNA and protein levels in keratinocytes, independently of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). The therapeutic efficacy of alnustone was evaluated in oxazolone-induced AD mouse model, where topical application significantly alleviated clinical severity, inflammation, and skin barrier defects. The molecular mechanism was explored using ChIP-seq data mining, isoform-specific modulation, promoter truncation, and DNA pull-down assays. The results demostrated that alnustone rebalanced p63 isoforms by downregulating the transcriptional repressor TAp63 and upregulating the transcriptional activator ΔNp63. Both isoforms directly bound to a core response element (-390/-381) within the FLG promoter to mediate its transcriptional activation. To our knowledge, alnustone represents the first barrier-repair agent that ameliorates AD by transcriptionally upregulating FLG via restoring TAp63/ΔNp63 homeostasis, offering a novel therapeutic strategy targeting skin barrier regeneration in AD.

articles.title: Aripiprazole collapses metabolic plasticity through the GNAQ/RXRα/MCT4 axis in colorectal cancer.
articles.abstract: Metabolic plasticity enables colorectal cancer (CRC) cells to adapt to energy stress by dynamically adjusting the relative contributions of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and glycolysis, thereby contributing to tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. However, pharmacological strategies capable of disrupting this metabolic flexibility remain limited. Here, we identify aripiprazole, an approved antipsychotic drug with emerging anticancer activity, as a disruptor of metabolic plasticity in CRC. Aripiprazole impaired mitochondrial function, reduced OXPHOS-derived ATP production, and initially triggered compensatory glycolytic activation. However, this adaptive response was not sustained, as aripiprazole suppressed monocarboxylate transporter 4 (MCT4), a key lactate transporter involved in glycolytic adaptation under hypoxic stress. Functional experiments showed that MCT4 overexpression attenuated aripiprazole-induced growth inhibition and apoptosis, whereas MCT4 knockdown sensitized CRC cells to hypoxic stress. Mechanistically, RXRα acted as a negative regulator of MCT4. Aripiprazole disrupted the interaction between GNAQ and RXRα, promoted nuclear accumulation of RXRα, thereby repressing MCT4 expression. This blockade of MCT4-dependent glycolytic compensation, together with mitochondrial dysfunction, resulted in ATP depletion and apoptotic cell death in CRC cells. Collectively, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized GNAQ/RXRα/MCT4 signaling axis that sustains metabolic plasticity in CRC and demonstrate that aripiprazole can pharmacologically disrupt this adaptive program. These results provide mechanistic insight into the anticancer activity of aripiprazole and support targeting metabolic plasticity as a therapeutic strategy for CRC.

articles.title: Vasorelaxant and Antihypertensive Effects of Salicylaldehyde: Involvement of Renin-Angiotensin System and Calcium/Potassium Channel Modulation.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Natural products are widely used in traditional medicine for managing cardiovascular disorders, including hypertension.
